newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan awaits Supreme Court verdict. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Pakistan awaits Supreme Court verdict. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]

text.p: Pakistanis waited anxiously on Tuesday for the Supreme Court to rule on ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto's plea for reinstatement.
The court was expected to announce its decision on Wednesday or Thursday, and if it rules in Bhutto's favour it could cause the cancellation of elections set for February 3.
Bhutto is demanding that the court overturn her November 5 dismissal by President Farooq Leghari, just as it rejected the presidential sacking of her main rival, Nawaz Sharif, in 1993.
Leghari dismissed Bhutto's government, alleging that its three years in power had been marked by corruption, nepotism, extra-judicial killings and contempt for the judiciary.

A seven-judge bench only began hearing Bhutto's appeal on January 13, after the Supreme Court (Corrects) had dismissed other challenges to the president's right to use constitutional powers to dismiss the elected National Assembly (lower house).

Uncertainty about the outcome has dampened an already lacklustre election campaign and induced caution among stock market investors who had been buying heavily on hopes that Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League would win the polls.
"No one is prepared to bet what the verdict will be," said dealer Salman Ahmad of Finex Securities as nervous profit-taking wiped off most early gains at the Karachi bourse on Tuesday.
The Karachi 100-share index rose 1.25 points, or 0.08 percent, to close at 1,503.41 after an early surge to 1,522.61.
Sikander Khawaja, chief representative of HSBC James Capel Asia Ltd, told Reuters that investors were staying away because they were unsure which way the Supreme Court would rule.
"Revival of the previous government would lead to further uncertainty, whatever the legal merits of the case," he said.

"Basically (it) would mean that all acts of the present government would become doubtful. There would again be polarisation between the president and the prime minister, and we might head for another period of instability.
"On the other hand, if elections do take place and one party or another wins a majority and a stable government is formed, that would be ideal for the market," Khawaja said.
Leghari himself has said that reinstatement of Bhutto's government would bring the election process to a halt.
And he told Cable News Network television on Monday that he might step down if the Supreme Court overturned his dismissal.
"Though it is not constitutionally binding on a president to resign, I might do so on moral grounds," Leghari said.

Speculation in the local media has suggested three options for the Supreme Court: to reject Bhutto's plea outright, to restore her government, or to uphold her plea but say the elections should go ahead anyway.
"Whatever happens, the ride is bound to be bumpy," wrote columnist Ghazi Salahuddin on Tuesday in the English-language daily The News. "Fasten your seat-belts."
